problem.paragraph: $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 4 - 2x - y$$ ; $$R = \left\{ {\left( {x,y} \right)\left| {0 \leq x \leq 1;0 \leq y \leq 2} \right.} \right\}$$
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x + y$$ ; $$R$$ is the triangle bounded by $$y = 2x$$ , $$y = 0$$ and $$x = 2$$ .
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ ; $$R$$ is the rectangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {1,0} \right),\left( {1,2} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ .
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = e^{x + 2y}$$ ; $$R$$ is the triangle with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ .
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2xe^{y}$$ ; $$R$$ is the triangle bounded by $$y = x$$ , $$y = 2$$ , and $$x = 0$$ .
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{2y}{1 + x^{2}}$$ ; $$R$$ is the region bounded by $$y = \sqrt{x}$$ , $$y = 0$$ , and $$x = 4$$ .
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2}y$$ ; $$R$$ is the region bounded by the graphs of $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^{2}$$ .
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x$$ ; $$R$$ is the region in the first quadrant bounded by the semicircle $$y = \sqrt{16 - x^{2}}$$ , the $$x$$ -axis, and the $$y$$ -axis.

exercises.instruction: In Exercises 28 and 29, determine whether the statement is true or false. If it is true, explain why it is true. If it is false, give an example to show why it is false.

problem.paragraph: Let $$R$$ be a region in the $$xy$$ -plane, and let $$f$$ and $$g$$ be continuous functions on $$R$$ that satisfy the condition $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \leq g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ for all $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$R$$ . Then,
$$\int_{R}{\int{\lbrack g(x,y) - f(x,y)\rbrack dA}}$$
gives the volume of the solid bounded above by the surface $$z = g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and below by the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ .

Suppose $$f$$ is nonnegative and continuous over the plane region $$R$$ . Then, the average value of $$f$$ over $$R$$ can be thought of as the (constant) height of the cylinder with base $$R$$ and volume that is exactly equal to the volume of the solid under the graph of $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ . (Note: The cylinder referred to here has sides perpendicular to $$R$$ .)
